questions.q: Which description best fits the EDA mindset?
options: Plot every possible chart and see what looks interesting
Hold a question, look for evidence, and let findings sharpen the next question
Fit a model first, then explore whatever it flags
Clean every column before looking at any distributions
questions.explain: EDA is question-driven and iterative. Plotting everything at random produces plots but no conclusions.

questions.q: Which set of checks belongs in the standard 'first look' at a new dataset?
options: Train/test split and cross-validation score
Correlation heatmap and pair plot only
Shape, data types, missing values, and duplicates
A dashboard with every column as a tile
questions.explain: Shape, dtypes (via info), missing counts, and duplicates tell you whether the data is even trustworthy before you draw anything.

questions.q: In the practice table, customers.duplicated().sum() printed 0 and info() showed age with 480 non-null values out of 500. What follows?
options: There are no duplicate rows, and 20 ages are missing
There are 20 duplicate rows and no missing values
480 customers have a valid age and the other 20 rows must be deleted
The dataset has 480 rows
questions.explain: A zero duplicate count means no exact duplicate rows; 500 minus 480 non-null ages leaves 20 missing values. Missing is not the same as delete: deciding what to do is a later step.

questions.q: describe() shows total_spend with a mean of 188.1, a median of 124.4, and a maximum of 9800. What is the best reading?
options: Everything is normal because the mean and median are both positive
The data must have been sorted incorrectly
The mean is being pulled up by skew or outliers, so investigate the top values
The median is wrong because it is smaller than the mean
questions.explain: When the mean sits well above the median and the max is huge, a long right tail or outliers are pulling the mean up. That is a cue to look at the distribution and the extreme rows.

questions.q: Why does the workflow treat EDA as a loop rather than a straight line?
options: Because pandas code has to be re-run after every edit
Because a surprising finding later often sends you back to re-check an earlier step
Because every dataset has to be explored exactly three times
Because stakeholders expect at least two drafts
questions.explain: A strange relationship in a two-variable view might send you back to check a single distribution, so the process cycles instead of running once.
